title: Kapila Teaches His Mother
word: each as a lens for a week
hookLine: Devahuti, worn out by wanting, asks her son Kapila how to be free: the second pair of lenses, Samkhya and Yoga
carry: samkhya and yoga: the seer is not the storm
tomorrow: a great debate, and two garlands.
last: A RELIABLE WORD, NOT A RUMOR.

lines: A MOTHER, WORN OUT BY WANTING.
TEACH ME HOW TO BE FREE.
cards: In the Bhagavata's third book, Devahuti has lived a long, full life. Her husband, the sage Kardama, has gone off to the forest. Her son stays with her.
His name is Kapila, and tradition remembers a sage named Kapila as the founder of Samkhya. One day she comes to him and says, in effect: I'm worn out by the cravings of my senses.
I've been lost in a darkness that won't lift. You've come to be my light. Teach me how to be free.
A son becomes his mother's teacher, and what he teaches is the second pair: Samkhya and Yoga.

teach.b: Kapila starts with the Samkhya question: who is watching? He draws the great division. On one side, prakriti, nature: everything that moves and changes, the body, the senses, even the mind and the sense of I.

On the other, purusha, the self, who sees and doesn't act. The trouble, he tells her, is that the self takes nature's movements as its own. Nature does the doing, and the self thinks: I am doing this, I am suffering this.

teach.h: THE MIND BINDS, THE MIND FREES.
teach.b: Then comes a line the Bhagavata is known for: the mind is the cause of bondage, and the mind is the cause of freedom. Tied to the world's pulls, it binds. Turned toward the Lord, it frees.
The Bhagavata's Kapila is a devotee as well as a philosopher; the classic Samkhya texts don't speak of God this way. Now the Yoga lens. Its question: what is the mind doing right now?
Patanjali's Yoga Sutra defines yoga as the stilling of the mind's movements. Then the seer rests in its own nature; otherwise it seems to take the mind's shapes. How do the movements settle?
By practice and by letting go.

teach.h: YOU ARE NOT YOUR PASSING STATES.
teach.b: That's the teaching under these two: in Hindu thought, you are not your passing states. Anger, fear, a speech building in your head: all of it is nature moving. The one who sees it isn't burning.
Devahuti, the Bhagavata says, practiced what her son taught her, and reached freedom.

how: Samkhya and Yoga are traditionally studied as a pair, and many Hindus first meet Samkhya's ideas in the Bhagavata, where Kapila teaches his mother Devahuti; the Yoga Sutra is the guide many use for stilling the mind.

games.q: what does “each as a lens for a week” mean?
o: seeing the storm as nature, and resting as the seer
holding anger in until it fades by itself
deciding that feeling anger means you've failed

p: asks her son how to be free
the cause of bondage, and of freedom

s: in Samkhya, the sense of I belongs to the witness
the I-maker sits on prakriti's side, with the senses and the mind.
in the Bhagavata, Kapila teaches Samkhya to his own mother
Devahuti asks how to be free, and her son answers.
the Yoga Sutra says the mind is stilled by willpower alone
it names two things together: practice and letting go.

games.q: your face goes hot at a careless word. you're using what Kapila taught Devahuti. what's the move?
o: decide you are the anger, and act on it.
see the anger as nature moving, rest as the one who sees, and turn the mind back.
push it down and pretend it never came.
games.why: Kapila: the self watches nature's movements; the mind binds when the world pulls it and frees when it's turned toward the Lord.

practice: Let a recent flash of anger or worry come to mind. With the Samkhya lens, notice that all of it, the heat, the story, even the I that was hurt, is being seen, and rest a few breaths as the one who sees.
With the Yoga lens, come back to your breath, stay a little longer than is easy, and loosen your grip on how it should have gone.
If you pray, turn that mind toward the One you pray to, as Kapila told his mother; if you don't, simply let it settle.

wordCard.voice: Each as a lens for a week. Today, the second pair: Samkhya asks who is watching, Yoga asks what the mind is doing. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: stilling, as in the Yoga Sutra's definition of yoga.

carryVoice: Your line: samkhya and yoga, the seer is not the storm. Kapila taught it to his own mother. Go gently.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 3.25 (Devahuti asks Kapila for release; the mind as the cause of bondage and of freedom, 3.25.15)
Bhagavata Purana 3.33 (Devahuti practices her son's teaching and reaches freedom)
Samkhya Karika (purusha the witness; prakriti and its unfolding, including the I-maker)
Yoga Sutra 1.2–1.4 (yoga as the stilling of the mind's movements; the seer rests in its own nature, otherwise takes their form)
Yoga Sutra 1.12–1.15 (the movements are stilled by practice and non-attachment; practice as effort toward steadiness; non-attachment as freedom from thirst for objects)
